overview: The difference is simply whether the body can synthesise the amino acid itself or must get it from food.
genZNote: Essential: must be delivered, the body can't cook this one up. Non-essential: the body's got a recipe for it already.

aspects.label: Can the Body Synthesise It?
aspects.valueA: No — must be obtained through diet.
aspects.valueB: Yes — the body can synthesise it internally from other compounds.

aspects.label: Number in Humans
aspects.valueA: 9 essential amino acids in adult humans (e.g. leucine, lysine, valine).
aspects.valueB: 11 non-essential amino acids (e.g. alanine, glutamine, glycine).

aspects.label: Dietary Importance
aspects.valueA: Deficiency requires dietary correction, especially important in protein-deficient diets.
aspects.valueB: Deficiency is rare unless there's an underlying metabolic disorder.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Some amino acids are 'conditionally essential' — normally non-essential but required from the diet during illness, infancy, or stress.
overlay.memoryTrick: Essential = 'essential to eat it', can't make it yourself.
overlay.commonMisconception: 'Non-essential' does not mean unimportant — both categories of amino acids are equally necessary for building proteins.
